claims.text: Selective chemical dealloying of an NM-HEA precursor can produce a three-dimensional porous nanoframework.
The resulting porous nanoframework exhibits enhanced catalytic performance.
High surface area and tunable atomic configuration cause the enhanced catalytic performance.
The NM-HEA precursor is uniformly alloyed and contains noble metals together with more reactive sacrificial elements.
A chemical etchant can preferentially dissolve the reactive elements from the precursor.
Mild, controlled acidic or alkaline etching can selectively remove reactive elements without collapsing the alloy structure.
Dealloying forms an interconnected porous network with nanoscale ligaments.
The nanoscale ligaments become enriched in noble metals.
Selective dissolution of sacrificial elements leaves behind a three-dimensional framework rich in noble-metal atoms.
Dealloying increases defect concentrations in the residual framework.
The dealloyed framework exposes more catalytically active sites.
The dealloyed nanoframework has greater surface area than the untreated NM-HEA.
The dealloyed nanoframework has better catalytic activity than the untreated NM-HEA.
The dealloyed nanoframework has better catalytic stability than the untreated NM-HEA.
Enhanced atomic-level control over active sites accounts for the improved catalytic activity and stability.
The untreated NM-HEA has a more bulk-uniform structure, lower effective surface area, and less controlled atomic-scale architecture.
Formation of the three-dimensional nanoframework requires precisely optimized etching conditions.
Overly aggressive etching can cause structural collapse.
Insufficient etching can produce inadequate porosity.
